title: Seventy Days
sub: Grades 5–8 · Science · How the Egyptians preserved a body

hero.credit: Facsimile by Charles K. Wilkinson, 1920–21 · The Met

objective: Students will follow the seventy days of mummification as the exhibition tells them, after the British Museum: eight steps, from washing to the coffin. They will read the room’s timeline as data, find that drying in natron took 40 of the 70 days, explain why taking out the moisture mattered, and design a fair test of drying with salt.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: People have kept things from rotting for thousands of years. The Egyptians’ seventy days are a careful process with a reason behind most steps, and asking why each step works is how a scientist thinks.

materials: Page 3 of this plan, projected or printed: the timeline and the eight steps
Differentiated handouts, one per student. *Optional, to run the test:* an apple, table salt, small cups, a kitchen scale
connection: **Virtual visit:** open *Mummification, Step by Step*. Do each of the eight steps by hand, then take the room’s three-question check.
**Poster 2**, *Gods and Goddesses*: Anubis, patron god of embalmers. Some pet cats were even mummified, to stay with their owners in the afterlife.

steps.title: Which step took longest?
script: Show the room and read its first line: *“The finest mummies took about seventy days to make.”* Ask students to guess, on their own, which step took longest, and to write one reason. Take a few guesses. Do not give the answer yet: *“Today we find out from the evidence, and then ask why.”*

screen.alt: The Mummification room: a simple figure lies on a wooden table above four canopic jars, beside a timeline of the seventy days and the step’s notes
screen.caption: Mummification, Step by Step

steps.purpose: Guess before anyone explains: which part of the seventy days took longest, and why?
students: The finest mummies took about seventy days. Which step do you think took longest?
Why would any step need weeks?

steps.title: Eight steps
script: Take the steps in order from page 3, plainly. Herodotus, a Greek historian who visited Egypt about 450 BC, gives the clearest written account; he says the most elaborate mummifications took 70 days. The brain was drawn out through the nose with a long bronze hook (the British Museum has one, made after 664 BC). The organs came out through a cut in the left side, were dried and wrapped, and went into four canopic jars, each protected by a god. **The heart was left inside:** the Egyptians thought it held a person’s will, feelings and thoughts.

screen.caption: The seventy days, step by step

cells: The body was washed, to make it pure.
The brain was removed through the nose with a long bronze hook, and it was not kept.
Each canopic jar had a protective god, one of the four Sons of Horus.
The organs came out through a cut in the left side. They were dried, wrapped and put in canopic jars.
Bags of natron, a natural salt, were packed inside and outside the body and left for 40 days, until all the moisture had gone.
The body was coated in resin and sweet-smelling oils, to help preserve it.
The linen was wrapped very carefully, with amulets between the layers to protect the body and spirit.
The mummy was ready to be placed in its coffin, or coffins, for the burial ceremony.

steps.purpose: Walk through the eight steps in order, plainly and gently.
students: Which steps were about cleaning or drying?

steps.title: Forty days out of seventy
script: Now the timeline. Students check their guesses: natron took **40 of the 70 days**, about 57%, a little more than half.

examples.title: What share of the seventy days was natron?
steps: Everything else together took the other 30 days.
examples.answer: A little more than half: about 57%

steps.purpose: Read the room’s timeline as data, and check the hook guesses.
students: What fraction of the time was left for everything else?

steps.title: What was the natron doing?
script: Read the natron note and underline *until all the moisture had gone*. Ask why drying might stop a body from decaying. Then give the general science, which is not from the exhibition: decay is mostly the work of tiny living things, and they need water. Take the water away and decay slows, which is why people have long salted and dried food.

students: What did the natron take away?
Why might a body that is dry last longer?

steps.title: Steps, data and a fair test
script: Students choose a handout. All three use the same steps and timeline and end with a salt test, predicted or planned. If you run it, slice one apple, pack some slices in table salt (standing in for natron) and leave others open, and compare them over a week. Nobody eats the slices.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Put the steps in order, find the longest step on the timeline, match each step to its job, and predict what salt will do to an apple slice.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Work out natron’s share of the seventy days, sort each material’s job as preserving or protecting by belief, and plan a fair test with one change, one measurement and what stays the same.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Argue a claim with evidence that drying did most to preserve the body, design a full fair test with a measurement and repeat trials, name its limits, and ask what evidence besides Herodotus could show how mummies were made.

steps.purpose: Work with the steps and the timeline, then plan a test of drying with salt, at the right level of challenge.
students: All three end by planning or predicting a test with salt.

steps.title: Testable, or belief?
script: Ask which steps a scientist could test today (washing, drying in natron, the resin and oils) and which were about belief (the jar gods, the amulets between the layers, the heart kept for the weighing). Both mattered to the embalmers: poster 2 calls Anubis, their patron god, gentle and caring, a god who made sure the dead were treated with respect.

screen.question: Which steps could a scientist test today? Which were about what the Egyptians believed?

steps.purpose: Separate what an experiment can check from what was a matter of belief, with respect for both.
students: Name one step you could test with an experiment.
Name one step that was about protection by the gods.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level student, who explains one variable in their fair test.
